abstract: This study investigated how artificial intelligence (AI) risk-taking tendencies and transparency design influence human risk-taking behavior, trust in AI, and neural activity in risky decision-making contexts. Drawing on previous findings of human–AI collaboration and social influence, we examined human–AI interaction during the Balloon Analogue Risk Task (BART), using functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) to measure cerebral activation. The study employed a 2 × 2 between-subjects design (risk-taking vs. conservative AI; transparent vs. non-transparent design). A total of 120 participants completed the task under one of four experimental conditions. Behavioral results showed that participants initially increased their risk-taking behavior when paired with risk-taking AI, but gradually reverted to baseline, indicating increasing risk-aversion over time. Conservative AI did not significantly reduce risk-taking behavior below baseline, though it elicited higher trust ratings. Contrary to predictions, similarity in risk-taking tendency did not significantly enhance trust. Transparency design accelerated risk-aversion toward risk-taking AI and reduced trust bias toward conservative AI. Neuroimaging results revealed decreases in prefrontal and temporoparietal junction oxygenated hemoglobin, consistent with cognitive offloading when AI advice was present; these effects were attenuated under the transparent condition, suggesting sustained engagement. Overall, findings highlight the dynamic nature of human–AI risk decision-making and underscore the role of transparency in calibrating trust and maintaining user involvement in risky decision-making tasks.

title: Human–AI Risk Decision-Making: The Effects of Risk-Taking Tendency and Transparency Design
title_zh: 人类–AI 风险决策：冒险倾向与透明度设计的影响
